newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African democracy at the school of hard knocks.
newsitem.headline: S. African democracy at the school of hard knocks.

text.p: Halfway through its five-year debut term South Africa's first democratic government is facing the sobering and expensive reality of its 1994 promise to eradicate centuries of white domination.
The nation still rallies with cheers and happy tears when revered 78-year-old President Nelson Mandela, who has vowed to retire in 1999, makes a call to unity and reconciliation.
But when he limps off to rest, the squabbling resumes both within his ruling African National Congress, and between the ANC and its rivals, over how to redesign a country skewed by white avarice.

"We've been sailing on the back of the miracle of the political transformation. Now we have hit the rock of economic transformation and it's very hard," Post, Telecommunications and Broadcasting Minister Jay Naidoo said in an interview.
"We're a lot more confident of ourselves and our policies than we were a year ago, but the job of turning this ship around is harder than we thought," he said.
Delivering the fruits of democracy to a five-to-one black majority remains the major challenge for Mandela's government.
Three days short of the November 10 halfway mark to elections in 1999, delegates wrapped up the parliamentary year on Thursday with South Africa's legislative framework significantly redesigned.
- The country's highest court is likely soon to ratify the final version of a brand new Constitution that will from January entrench the rights and equality that apartheid denied.

- Finance Minister Trevor Manuel piloted a macro-economic policy through cabinet that repudiates the ANC's traditional policies in favour of an orthodox market-driven strategy for growth and the war against unemployment of over 30 percent.
- A new education act wipes out the last legal protection for whites against the dominance of a vast and largely poor black majority now guaranteed an equal share of all resources.
- Hard-fought decisions to liberalise abortion and scrap censorship marked a victory for progressive ideology over the Calvinist Afrikaner morals that shaped apartheid.

"We've done a lot better than last year - we're learning how things work in government and in parliament - but we have found that our ideals have had to be tempered with reality," Public Works Minister Jeff Radebe told Reuters.
A recent Human Sciences Research Council poll showed 51 percent of the population dissatisfied to very dissatisfied with the economy and only 33 percent at all happy with it.
"I would give them six out of 10 or a Beta minus," said University of Cape Town political analyst David Welsh.
"All this dithering over policy - there's been lots of talk, but we have yet to see these policies put to work," he said.

The year began with power uncomfortably shared by Mandela's ANC and the white-led National Party of former president F.W. de Klerk, who, in 1990, repudiated his people's belief in white superiority and set the stage for a transition to democracy.

In May, after parliament's adoption of a draft constitution that made no place for power-sharing, de Klerk announced he would withdraw from the government of national unity. He did so in June, leaving Mandela alone in power with a small contingent of the conservative Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party.
National Party Secretary General Roelf Meyer said he shared Welsh's concerns about delivery and about what both men saw as the first signs of intolerant autocracy.
"We're still halfway through the political transformation and much has still to happen.... Not much has changed in this country yet, not for either side," Meyer said.
